title: System Technologies Inc. v. Commissioner
articleTitle: Comprehensive Legal and Economic Analysis of System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner (Docket No. 12211-21) and the Funded Research Exception
subject: Funded Research Exclusion
summary: A procedural Tax Court order addressing evidence, discovery, and substantiation standards for Section 41 QRE eligibility.

body.text: Introduction to the Evolving Landscape of Research and Development Tax Controversy

The federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities, codified under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41, serves as a cornerstone of United States corporate tax policy, expressly designed to incentivize domestic technological innovation and enhance the global competitiveness of American industries. By providing a dollar-for-dollar reduction in federal income tax liability, the research and development (R&D) credit significantly alters the economic calculus of corporate investments in research and experimental activities. However, as the financial magnitude of these corporate claims has grown substantially over the past decade, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has subjected them to intense administrative scrutiny, resulting in a highly adversarial tax controversy environment characterized by rigorous demands for contemporaneous documentation and the aggressive enforcement of statutory exclusions.

Among the most heavily litigated of these statutory exclusions is the "funded research" limitation, codified under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H). This provision disqualifies research expenditures from generating a tax credit to the extent that the research is funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity. The determination of whether research is legally classified as "funded" relies on an exceptionally complex analysis of contractual risk allocation and the retention of intellectual property rights. Traditionally, this analysis was evaluated strictly within the "four corners" of the commercial agreements governing the research, creating significant vulnerabilities for government contractors, engineering firms, and bespoke manufacturers whose commercial contracts lacked explicit tax-centric language.

The United States Tax Court proceedings in System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, No. 12211-21 (T.C. 2025), represent a critical and highly informative juncture in the jurisprudence of the funded research exclusion. The series of orders issued by Judge Ronald L. Buch in January and February 2025 illustrate the intricate intersection of federal tax law, state commercial law, and stringent pre-trial discovery standards in the modern tax litigation landscape. The Court's denial of the Commissioner's Motion for Partial Summary Judgment on the funded research issue established a pivotal precedent, affirming that when commercial contracts are silent on the specific financial remedies for the total failure of a research project, state law gap-fillers—such as the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC)—can govern the allocation of financial risk, thereby preserving a taxpayer's eligibility for the R&D credit.

Concurrently, the Tax Court's subsequent orders granting the Commissioner's Motions to Compel Responses to Interrogatories highlight the unforgiving nature of the substantive procedural requirements necessary to validate qualified research activities. Together, these rulings provide a comprehensive blueprint of modern R&D tax litigation. They demonstrate that while sophisticated contract interpretation and the strategic application of state commercial law can successfully overcome statutory exclusions, a taxpayer's ultimate success depends entirely on their ability to produce granular, project-specific evidentiary documentation substantiating the scientific process of experimentation.

This report provides an exhaustive, multi-dimensional analysis of the System Technologies litigation. It dissects the factual background of the taxpayer, the statutory mechanics of the funded research exclusion, the novel application of state commercial law to federal tax disputes, and the stringent evidentiary standards currently governing the process of experimentation. Furthermore, the report contextualizes these rulings within contemporary jurisprudence, comparing them extensively to parallel appellate and Tax Court decisions such as Smith v. Commissioner and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, and outlines the broader macro-tax implications for corporate taxpayers navigating IRS examinations in 2025 and 2026.
The Statutory Architecture of the R&D Credit and the Funded Research Exclusion

To accurately analyze the legal maneuvers in the System Technologies litigation, it is necessary to first examine the foundational statutory and regulatory architecture of the federal research credit. Under IRC Section 41, the computation of the research credit is mathematically expressed as a percentage of the taxpayer's qualified research expenses (QREs) for a given tax year that exceed a statutorily defined historical base amount. The qualifying expenditures are strictly limited by statute to three primary components: in-house research expenses paid as wages to employees for performing qualified services, the cost of raw materials and supplies utilized directly in the conduct of qualified research, and a statutorily limited percentage (typically 65 percent) of contract research expenses paid to third-party entities.

However, the identification and inclusion of these expenditures as eligible QREs is only permissible if the underlying research activities satisfy a stringent, conjunctive four-part standard, commonly known in tax jurisprudence as the "Four-Part Test". The Internal Revenue Service relies entirely on these four fundamental characteristics to separate eligible, qualified research from non-qualifying, routine engineering, standard business development, or reverse-engineering activities.

The first requirement is the Permitted Purpose Test, which mandates that the expenditures must be eligible for treatment as specified research or experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174. This requires that the activity be intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component, specifically regarding its reliability, quality, performance, or function. The term "business component" is statutorily defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business.

The second requirement is the Technological in Nature Test. This standard dictates that the process of experimentation used to discover the necessary information must fundamentally rely on principles of the "hard sciences," such as the physical sciences, biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. This test explicitly excludes research grounded in the social sciences, arts, or humanities.

The third requirement is the Elimination of Uncertainty Test, which dictates that at the outset of the development project, the taxpayer must face technological uncertainty concerning the capability or method of developing the business component, or the optimal design of the business component itself. The IRS strictly interprets this to mean that routine adaptations of existing technologies where the outcome is generally known do not qualify.

The fourth and final requirement is the Process of Experimentation Test. This rigorous standard requires that substantially all of the research activities must constitute a structured, scientific process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities. Recent judicial interpretations have established a rigid quantitative threshold, determining that at least eighty percent of the activities must constitute this structured process.

If an engineering or scientific activity successfully navigates this highly restrictive four-part matrix, it faces a secondary gauntlet of statutory exclusions outlined in IRC Section 41(d)(4). These exclusions prohibit taxpayers from claiming the credit for research conducted after the beginning of commercial production, the adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement, the duplication of an existing business component, routine surveys and studies, foreign research, and most critically for commercial contractors, funded research.
Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d): The Allocation of Economic Risk

The legislative intent behind the funded research exclusion is foundational to preventing the federal government from subsidizing research efforts where the taxpayer does not bear the true economic risk of failure. The underlying economic philosophy is that if a third party, such as a client or a governmental agency, agrees to pay for the research regardless of its ultimate outcome, that third party is the entity bearing the financial risk, and thus, the third party is the entity logically entitled to claim the resulting R&D tax credit.

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d) operationalizes this statutory exclusion through a two-pronged test. Research is considered "funded"—and therefore entirely ineligible for the federal credit for the performing taxpayer—if either of two conditions are met. First, the research is funded if the payment for the research is not contingent on the success of the research. Second, the research is funded if the taxpayer does not retain substantial rights in the results of the research.

In the context of the System Technologies litigation, the Commissioner's Motion for Partial Summary Judgment focused exclusively on the first prong: the assertion that payment was not contingent on the success of the research. Under the regulatory framework, if an engineering firm operates under a fixed-fee contract where progress payments are guaranteed upon the delivery of intermediate milestones, and there is no explicit contractual mechanism requiring the firm to refund those payments if the final technical design fails to operate, the IRS deems the research to be funded. To defeat this presumption, the contractor must demonstrate a binding legal requirement to bear the financial burden of redesign, remediation, or total contractual failure.
Factual Background and Procedural Posture of System Technologies

System Technologies, Inc. is a specialized engineering and manufacturing corporation headquartered in Indianapolis, Indiana. The company operates primarily within the automotive manufacturing supply chain, offering deep expertise in the design, engineering, and fabrication of custom industrial finishing systems. The firm's highly technical portfolio encompasses automated automotive coating designs and applications, pre-treatment cleansing solutions, high-velocity blow-off and cool-off systems, ultraviolet curing applications, automatic liquid or powder systems, and highly complex robotic paint application architectures. The development of these bespoke industrial systems routinely necessitates the resolution of unique engineering challenges tailored to the specific geometric, chemical, thermodynamic, and operational requirements of individual automotive components.

The tax controversy at the center of this litigation originated from System Technologies' strategic decision to file amended federal corporate income tax returns for the consecutive tax years of 2015, 2016, 2017, and 2018. The core driver of these return amendments was a newly claimed research credit pursuant to IRC Section 41 for the 2016 tax year, quantifying $99,304 in generated tax credits. Because the total value of the 2016 credit significantly exceeded the company's baseline corporate income tax liability for that specific year, which amounted to $46,307, the statutory carryback and carryforward provisions of the Internal Revenue Code were subsequently triggered. System Technologies legally utilized $46,307 to offset its 2016 liability, carried the remaining credit balance backward to successfully absorb its outstanding 2015 tax liability, and subsequently carried the unresolved remainder forward to the 2017 and 2018 tax years, ultimately absorbing those liabilities and leaving a nominal unused credit balance of $1,118.

The foundational $99,304 credit was entirely predicated on the aggregation of QREs incurred during the intense development of six specific, customized industrial finishing systems engineered and fabricated during the 2016 operational year.

body.text: Each of these six engineering projects was executed pursuant to comprehensive commercial proposals, formal purchase orders, and subsequent sales agreements. Crucially, each of these governing agreements incorporated a standard, uniform choice-of-law provision explicitly stating that the contract would be strictly construed under and governed by the laws of the State of Indiana.

Upon receiving and reviewing the amended tax returns, the Internal Revenue Service initiated an exhaustive examination that culminated in the issuance of a statutory notice of deficiency to System Technologies on March 25, 2021. The Commissioner took the aggressive stance of wholly disallowing the $99,304 research credit claimed for 2016. Because the 2016 credit had been utilized across multiple years, this total disallowance consequently resulted in the assessment of corporate tax deficiencies across all four impacted tax years (2015 through 2018) due to the systemic reversal of the carrybacks and carryforwards. In response to this existential threat to their tax strategy, System Technologies filed a formal petition with the United States Tax Court to redetermine the deficiencies, plunging the parties into a protracted and highly adversarial period of formal and informal discovery.
The Summary Judgment Dispute: Contractual Silence vs. State Commercial Law

On August 1, 2024, as the case progressed toward a scheduled special trial session in Indianapolis, Indiana, the Commissioner filed a formal Motion for Partial Summary Judgment. The IRS requested that the Tax Court rule, as a matter of law, that the research conducted across the six disputed projects by System Technologies constituted "funded research" within the meaning of IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H), thereby disqualifying the entirety of the claimed QREs.
The Commissioner's Argument: Exclusive Remedies and the Doctrine of Remoteness

The IRS grounded its motion in a strict, literal, "four-corners" reading of the commercial agreements executing the six projects. The purchase agreements for these massive industrial systems inherently mandated structured progress payments as the engineering and fabrication phases advanced toward completion. To establish that the taxpayer bore no financial risk, the Commissioner highlighted two primary legal theories:

First, the IRS emphasized the complete absence of express contingency clauses. The agency noted that the purchase orders and subcontractor agreements entirely lacked any explicit contractual language conditioning the client's obligation to pay on the successful completion of the underlying research and engineering.

Second, the IRS relied heavily on the exclusivity of the warranty provisions embedded within the agreements. The contracts contained standard, limited commercial warranty clauses wherein System Technologies guaranteed that the manufactured equipment would be free from defects in material and workmanship under normal operational use. Crucially, the warranty stipulated that in the event of a breach, System Technologies' sole and exclusive obligation was limited to the commitment to "repair or replace free of charge such defective parts". The warranty further declared in standard boilerplate language that this specific remedy was "exclusive, and in lieu of all other warranties, whether written, oral, or implied".

The IRS forcefully argued that these provisions entirely shielded System Technologies from the ultimate financial risk of development failure. According to the Commissioner's interpretation, if the experimental research failed and the system did not function as intended, the firm was merely obligated to repair or replace individual parts, not to refund the client's millions of dollars in progress payments. Furthermore, the Commissioner advanced a sophisticated "remoteness" argument, contending that a total failure to deliver the industrial system was not a realistic or probable outcome. Because both commercial parties fully expected successful delivery and structured their progress payments reflecting that absolute confidence, the theoretical economic risk of non-delivery was deemed too remote to satisfy the regulatory "contingent on success" requirement.
The Taxpayer's Defense: The Gap-Filling Power of the Uniform Commercial Code

System Technologies countered the IRS's rigid, text-bound contractual interpretation by strategically invoking the choice-of-law provisions deeply embedded in all of the project proposals. Because the contracts explicitly mandated governance by the laws of the State of Indiana, the taxpayer's legal counsel argued that the Tax Court's analysis could not be artificially confined to the explicit text of the documents. Instead, the analysis must comprehensively incorporate the default statutory rights, protections, and remedies afforded to buyers under the Indiana enactment of the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC).

The taxpayer readily conceded the factual point that the contracts were entirely silent regarding the specific financial remedy available if System Technologies failed entirely to deliver a completed, functioning product. However, under Indiana commercial law, contractual silence does not extinguish a buyer's inherent rights.

Specifically, the taxpayer relied upon the statutory authority of Indiana Code § 26-1-2-711(1), a powerful provision dictating that if a seller fails to make delivery or repudiates the contract, the buyer possesses a statutory right to cancel the contract entirely and recover or refund "so much of the price as has been paid". Therefore, System Technologies argued that if their extensive research and engineering efforts failed entirely, rendering them incapable of delivering the automated finishing systems, the clients possessed an absolute, unyielding statutory right to demand a full refund of all progress payments, regardless of the contract's silence on the matter.
The Tax Court's Landmark Ruling (January 3, 2025)

Judge Ronald L. Buch issued a comprehensive order on January 3, 2025, systematically dismantling the Commissioner's legal theories and officially denying the motion for partial summary judgment. The Court's deep analysis represents a masterclass in navigating the highly technical interplay between federal tax administration regulations and state property and contract law.

The Court directly addressed the IRS's central argument that the "repair or replace" warranty constituted the exclusive remedy available to the buyer, which theoretically precluded any right to a financial refund. Judge Buch meticulously analyzed this contention under the framework of Indiana Code § 26-1-2-719, the specific state statute governing the contractual modification or limitation of commercial remedies. While the UCC broadly allows parties to contractually limit remedies, Indiana state law strictly construes such limitations against the seller and firmly mandates that contracts must provide "at least minimally adequate remedies".

Judge Buch applied the critical safeguard doctrine found in Indiana Code § 26-1-2-719(2), which establishes that if circumstances cause an exclusive or limited remedy to "fail of its essential purpose," the default statutory remedies of the UCC are immediately and fully restored to the buyer. The Court logically reasoned that if System Technologies' research failed entirely, resulting in a total inability to deliver a functioning finishing system (constituting a total breach of contract), a limited warranty promising only to "repair or replace defective parts" would be rendered entirely meaningless. A commercial seller inherently cannot repair parts of a complex machine that does not exist or fundamentally fails to operate as designed. Consequently, the limited remedy would fail of its essential purpose, and the buyer's rights would automatically default back to the statutory right to a full refund of all progress payments under Indiana Code § 26-1-2-711. Because the buyer could legally claw back the expended funds upon a total research failure through state-level protections, the payment to System Technologies was legally and practically contingent on the success of the research.

Furthermore, addressing the IRS's assertion that non-delivery was an unrealistic or remote outcome, the Court firmly established the procedural boundaries of summary judgment review. The Court noted that at the summary judgment stage, judicial procedure dictates that it must draw all factual inferences in the light most favorable to the non-moving party, which in this instance was System Technologies.

More critically from a substantive tax law perspective, Judge Buch clarified a fundamental distinction between the "funded research" exclusion and the separate "technical uncertainty" requirement. The high probability of technical success in an engineering project might indeed threaten a taxpayer's ability to prove the existence of technical uncertainty at the outset of the project, which is required under the Four-Part Test. However, the probability of ultimate success has absolutely no bearing on the legal realities of contractual risk allocation. Whether a catastrophic failure is highly likely or highly remote, the sole legal question under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1) is identifying which party bears the financial burden if that failure ultimately occurs. By ruling that Indiana state law established the financial risk firmly upon the taxpayer, Judge Buch confirmed that System Technologies' research was not funded, thereby preserving their right to defend the validity of the credits at a full trial.
Evidentiary Burdens and the Procedural Discovery Phase: The Motions to Compel

While System Technologies secured a massive, highly publicized victory regarding the legal mechanics of the funded research exclusion, the ensuing pre-trial discovery phase exposed severe structural vulnerabilities in the taxpayer's ability to substantively document their research activities. On February 21, 2025, the Tax Court issued a subsequent order directly addressing two separate Motions to Compel Responses to Interrogatories filed by the Commissioner.

This February order provides profound insights into the IRS's current, highly aggressive audit methodology and demonstrates the Tax Court's zero-tolerance policy for evasive, high-level, or generalized discovery responses in complex Section 41 litigation.
The Stringent Standard for Discovery in Tax Court Proceedings

The discovery dispute between System Technologies and the Commissioner was governed by specific, highly demanding Tax Court Rules of Practice and Procedure. Tax Court Rule 70(b) explicitly permits the broad discovery of any non-privileged matter that is relevant to the subject of the pending case, placing the heavy burden of proving irrelevance firmly on the objecting party, a standard upheld in historical precedent such as Rosenfeld v. Commissioner, 82 T.C. 105 (1984). Furthermore, Rule 71(b) dictates that interrogatory responses must be formulated in good faith and answered as completely as the answering party's information permits, necessitating a reasonable and thorough inquiry. Crucially, Rule 104 empowers the Tax Court to formally compel answers and impose severe sanctions if a party provides an "evasive or incomplete" response.

The substantive legal backdrop justifying the Commissioner's exhaustively detailed discovery requests was the statutory "Process of Experimentation" standard. Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) strictly defines this process as one designed to evaluate one or more alternatives where the capability, method, or appropriate design is deeply uncertain at the very start of the research endeavor, a definition heavily enforced in recent cases such as Siemer Milling Company v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37.
Analysis of the First Motion to Compel (Filed January 24, 2025)

The Commissioner's first motion heavily targeted Interrogatories 8 and 10, which sought to dissect the exact nature of the technological uncertainty and the methodological experimentation applied uniquely to each specific business component claimed by the taxpayer.

Interrogatory 10 explicitly demanded that System Technologies describe the process of experimentation in granular detail and produce all corporate documents supporting four distinct elements: the initial scientific hypothesis, the specific testing utilized to test that identified hypothesis, the hard data collected from the testing iterations, and a narrative explaining how the testing results were ultimately utilized to finalize the design.

System Technologies objected to these intense requests, characterizing them as "cumulative and repetitive." In their submitted responses, rather than identifying the specific uncertainties and hypotheses for each individual machine engineered (such as detailing the fluid dynamics issues within the high-pressure hydroflush cells developed for the Gosiger Project), the taxpayer provided a generalized, high-level corporate overview of how the company methodically resolves uncertainties as a standard business practice, casually referring the IRS to broad project proposal documents.

The Tax Court unequivocally rejected this evasive approach. Citing the statutory requirement that the Four-Part Test must be applied independently and strictly at the business component level, the Court ruled that offering a generalized narrative of standard operating procedures is legally and procedurally insufficient. The taxpayer is required to map the specific scientific hypotheses, testing variables, and collected empirical data directly to the exact business component generating the QREs.
Analysis of the Second Motion to Compel (Filed January 31, 2025)

The Commissioner's second motion to compel exposed even deeper flaws in the taxpayer's operational ability to substantiate critical wage allocations and technical engineering specifications during the 2016 tax year.

body.text: Judge Buch granted both motions in full, firmly ordering System Technologies to supplement their answers and provide complete, detailed, non-evasive responses to both sets of interrogatories by the strict deadline of March 14, 2025.

The stark dichotomy between the two judicial orders in this case is highly illuminating for tax practitioners. While the January order demonstrated a favorable, highly pragmatic interpretation of state commercial law to protect taxpayers from the absolute disqualification of the funded research exclusion, the February order reinforced a draconian, uncompromising adherence to strict evidentiary standards. The implication for corporate taxpayers is resoundingly clear: brilliant legal defenses regarding contractual risk allocation are rendered entirely moot if the taxpayer's engineering and accounting departments cannot produce contemporaneous documentation proving that they formed scientific hypotheses, meticulously tested alternatives, and tracked their employee time accurately. The explicit rejection of "post-hoc time estimates" derived from retroactive tax studies and the dismissal of standard engineering specification sheets as substitutes for actual experimental documentation perfectly aligns with a broader judicial trend heavily punishing taxpayers who rely on reconstructed narratives.
Comparative Jurisprudence and the Evolution of the Funded Research Doctrine

The immense significance of the System Technologies rulings is best understood when deeply contextualized against the prevailing jurisprudence shaping the R&D tax credit landscape throughout 2024, 2025, and into 2026. The Tax Court is actively refining the boundaries of the funded research exclusion, requiring tax professionals to analyze a vast matrix of competing precedents.
Aligning with Smith v. Commissioner (T.C. Order 2024)

The highly technical legal mechanics successfully employed by the taxpayer in System Technologies closely mirror those utilized in the contemporaneous and heavily cited Tax Court case Smith v. Commissioner (Docket Nos. 13382-17, 13385-17, and 13387-17). The Smith litigation centered on the shareholders of Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture, LLP (AS+GG), a prestigious Chicago-based architectural firm globally renowned for designing sustainable, supertall, and highly complex architectural structures requiring massive amounts of preliminary research. The IRS aggressively disallowed the firm's R&D credits across several highly complex international design projects, including the Atrium City Tower, Kingdom Tower, and Masdar HQ, arguing that the architectural research was fully funded because payment was guaranteed and the firm allegedly did not retain substantial rights to the designs, retaining only incidental "institutional knowledge".

Similar to the contractual environment in System Technologies, the underlying commercial contracts in Smith lacked explicit, tax-centric language dictating financial risk and intellectual property ownership. However, because the projects were massive international developments, the contracts were governed entirely by foreign law—specifically, the commercial laws of Dubai and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The taxpayers masterfully argued that under UAE law, intellectual property rights and copyrights automatically vest in the original creator (the architect) unless explicitly and formally forfeited, thereby entirely satisfying the "substantial rights" prong of the funded research exclusion. Furthermore, the Tax Court clarified a crucial procedural element in Smith, stating that Tax Court Rule 146 does not require a taxpayer to file a separate formal notice of intent to rely upon foreign law when the IRS is already intimately aware of its relevance to the contracts in dispute.

The Tax Court decisively denied the IRS's motion for summary judgment in Smith, asserting that the interpretation of foreign commercial law and its direct application to the contractual milestone payments created genuine, profound issues of material fact that necessitated a full trial. When viewed together as a cohesive legal strategy, Smith and System Technologies establish a highly robust defense blueprint for corporate taxpayers: when the "four corners" of a commercial contract are ambiguous or entirely silent regarding strict R&D regulatory requirements, taxpayers can and should aggressively leverage the default provisions of the governing local, state, or foreign law to establish their financial risk and intellectual property retention.
Contrasting with Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner (8th Cir. 2024)

Conversely, the taxpayer victory in System Technologies acts as a vital counterbalance to the highly detrimental precedent established for contractors in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. (MBJ) v. Commissioner. In the MBJ decision, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals firmly upheld the Tax Court's decision denying massive research credits to a structural engineering firm. The firm operated under standard fixed-fee contracts where payment was reliably tied to the delivery of standard design documents.

The critical distinction separating System Technologies from MBJ lies in the exact nature of the financial risk borne by the taxpayer. In MBJ, the appellate courts found that if the architectural or structural designs contained technical errors, the firm was merely required to revise the drawings—a process that incurred nominal labor costs but did not threaten the underlying contract payment stream or legally require the firm to refund the client. Because the firm's true economic risk was limited merely to absorbing the internal cost of extra hours spent fixing drawings, rather than a catastrophic contractual obligation to return millions of dollars in progress payments for a completely failed product, the Eighth Circuit confidently ruled the research was funded.

System Technologies survived the IRS's motion for summary judgment precisely because the physical nature of their deliverables (massive industrial machinery) and the specific mechanics of the Indiana UCC exposed them to the severe, catastrophic economic risk of issuing total refunds—a level of risk the structural engineers in MBJ simply did not face.

This critical nuance regarding the scale of economic risk traces its jurisprudential origins back to the landmark Federal Circuit decision in Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States (71 F.3d 868, 1995), which originally established the doctrine that fixed-price contracts retain true risk for the taxpayer only if the taxpayer is unequivocally required to foot the entire bill for ultimate project failure. The continuing relevance of these doctrines is further evidenced by a slew of recent decisions throughout 2023 and 2024, including Moore v. Commissioner (affirming credits for scoreboard design where CEO wages were properly allocated), Grigsby v. United States (reversing a district denial of architectural projects), Phoenix Design Group, Inc. (denying credits for lacking documentation of experimentation), and Intermountain Electronics Inc. (allowing credits for electrical systems design), all of which point to a hyper-active litigation environment surrounding the R&D credit.
Administrative Scrutiny, Tax Form Revisions, and Capitalization Rules

The immense judicial scrutiny applied by the Tax Court in cases like System Technologies must also be analyzed in direct conjunction with the massive administrative and regulatory overhaul currently being executed by the IRS regarding R&D credit claims in 2025 and beyond.

The strict discovery posture observed in the February 2025 order perfectly mirrors the highly aggressive administrative stance the IRS adopted in late 2021 when it released Field Attorney Advice (FAA) 20214101F. This directive mandated that any corporate taxpayer filing an amended return to claim an R&D credit refund must provide exhaustive documentation identifying all business components, specifying all research activities performed, and detailing the exact scientific information sought to be discovered. While the IRS recently provided minor relief by waiving the requirement to provide individual employee names on claims postmarked after June 18, 2024, the fundamental, unyielding demand for highly granular, component-by-component substantiation remains fully enforced throughout all active audits. Furthermore, the IRS has extended the administrative transition period allowing taxpayers 45 days to correct deficient claims through January 10, 2026, indicating a long-term commitment to these rigorous reporting standards.

This intense administrative philosophy has now been permanently codified into the corporate tax return itself. In January 2025, the IRS published the finalized, highly controversial version of Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities), introducing sweeping new mandatory disclosure requirements. The newly mandated Schedule G, which is optional for 2024 but strictly mandatory for the 2025 tax year (and mandatory immediately for qualified small businesses offsetting payroll taxes), requires taxpayers to explicitly list their research projects by individual business component, provide short, detailed narrative descriptions of the specific scientific hypotheses sought to be discovered, and map exact QREs to each specific component. System Technologies' catastrophic failure in the discovery phase—specifically its inability to map unique technical uncertainties and specific experimental processes to the ten individual hydroflush cells comprising the Gosiger Project—represents the exact generalized reporting behavior the IRS designed Schedule G to eradicate completely.

Finally, the pursuit of the R&D credit is further complicated by the ongoing mandatory capitalization requirements of IRC Section 174. Effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) eliminated the historical right to immediately expense Specified Research or Experimental (SRE) expenditures. Taxpayers are now required to capitalize and amortize these costs over five years for domestic research (and fifteen years for foreign research). Because the Permitted Purpose Test of the Section 41 R&D credit requires that an expense first legally qualify as an SRE under Section 174, the definitions and their resulting tax treatments are inextricably linked. The IRS announced a massive new enforcement campaign in December 2024, targeting taxpayers who blatantly disregarded Section 174 capitalization while waiting to see if legislation like the proposed One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) of 2025 would reinstate immediate expensing. If a taxpayer successfully argues that their activities meet the technological uncertainty tests to secure the Section 41 credit, they simultaneously and irreversibly lock themselves into the mandatory amortization requirements of Section 174 for those exact same expenses, creating a highly complex economic modeling scenario for corporate tax departments.
Strategic Directives and Macro-Tax Implications for Corporate Taxpayers

The adjudicatory outcomes resulting from the System Technologies litigation precipitate significant, paradigm-shifting ripple effects for corporate tax planning, commercial contract structuring, and tax controversy management.

The most immediate practical takeaway from the January 2025 order is the paramount importance of the choice-of-law provision in commercial contracting. Historically, corporations and their legal departments viewed these provisions as mere legal boilerplate, often prioritizing jurisdictions with highly favorable corporate governance statutes or predictable litigation venues, such as Delaware or New York. However, the System Technologies precedent dictates that corporate tax departments must now actively collaborate with corporate counsel during the drafting phase to evaluate exactly how a selected jurisdiction's commercial code interacts with federal tax statutes regarding risk allocation.

For heavy manufacturers, engineering firms, and industrial designers, proactively selecting state jurisdictions that strictly interpret UCC gap-fillers regarding refund rights for non-delivery can inadvertently save a massive R&D credit claim if the contract itself lacks explicit "contingent on success" language. Conversely, for software developers and professional services firms where UCC Article 2 (governing the Sale of Goods) may not strictly apply, firms must be vastly more explicit in drafting contractual clauses that force the firm to definitively bear the cost of redesign and explicitly permit the client to withhold or demand the return of funds if technological milestones are not successfully achieved.

Simultaneously, the February 2025 discovery orders absolutely mandate an enhancement of contemporaneous documentation protocols. Corporations can no longer safely rely on high-level R&D studies based on post-hoc executive interviews or percentage-based wage allocations applied broadly across engineering departments. The standard expected by both the IRS and the Tax Court is now contemporaneous, project-level, component-by-component scientific and financial tracking.
Conclusion

The litigation in System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner stands as a defining, highly instructive case study in the modern, ultra-competitive era of federal tax controversy. The United States Tax Court's January 2025 order denying summary judgment decisively affirmed that taxpayers possess the strategic ability to utilize state commercial law and default UCC provisions to defeat the IRS's historically rigid application of the funded research exclusion. By astutely recognizing that the "failure of essential purpose" doctrine effectively places the ultimate financial risk of non-delivery squarely on the manufacturer, the Court provided a vital legal lifeline to engineering and manufacturing firms operating under standard commercial purchase orders.

However, the Court's subsequent February 2025 discovery orders serve as a stark, unavoidable warning: brilliant, sophisticated legal defenses regarding contract interpretation and state law risk allocation are entirely hollow if the taxpayer lacks the evidentiary substantiation required to prove the substantive elements of the research itself. The judicial dismissal of high-level tax studies, percentage-based wage allocations, and general engineering specifications in favor of granular, component-specific scientific documentation highlights the intense, almost insurmountable burden of proof facing corporate taxpayers who fail to track their R&D in real-time.

As the Internal Revenue Service rapidly operationalizes these strict standards through the mandatory deployment of Schedule G on Form 6765 and heightens its enforcement of Section 174 capitalization rules, corporate taxpayers must fundamentally restructure their entire approach to R&D compliance. Success in claiming and defending the federal research credit in 2025 and beyond now demands seamless, continuous integration between a corporation's legal department (for choice-of-law and risk allocation contracting), its engineering divisions (for contemporaneous scientific documentation), and its tax professionals (for component-level financial tracking).
